title: Should You Buy the Extended Warranty? Here's the Honest Answer
summary: A 28-year car-finance veteran explains what a vehicle service contract really is, how dealer markup and outside quotes work, and when buying one actually makes sense.

assertions.quote: An extended warranty is not actually a warranty. It is a service contract
you can typically cancel it and get a pro-rated refund back

verdicts.note: Common contract term, though cancellation fees and processing delays are also commonly reported.

CFPB examiners describe add-on products including vehicle service contracts and GAP as "a cancellable, pro-rata-refundable add-on product," confirming this is the norm the agency found violations against.

assertions.quote: My credit union already quoted me $1,900 for this exact coverage
Extended warranties tend to be more expensive on brands with a history of more frequent or more expensive repairs

verdicts.note: Matches Consumer Reports' survey finding that less reliable brands paid more for coverage.

assertions.quote: It does not cover brake pads that wore down from normal driving

verdicts.note: A standard, well-documented feature of these contracts across both auto and appliance plans.

assertions.quote: I would recommend one if you do not have extra cash flow sitting available throughout the year for a surprise repair bill

verdicts.note: A reasonable framework from an insider, though it still depends heavily on which specific vehicle and plan are involved.

assertions.quote: leased vehicles are typically still under factory coverage for the length of the lease anyway

verdicts.note: Straightforward consequence of lease terms typically being shorter than factory coverage.

assertions.quote: A third-party company is actually backing that warranty

verdicts.note: Described directly by the source as an industry insider.

Lee & Venkataraman note extended warranties sold by dealers are commonly underwritten by "well-established third-party warranty companies such as GE Capital, Lubrico, Global, and Pafco" -- consistent with a handful of third-party backers behind dealer-sold contracts, though the paper doesn't address bank-sold contracts specifically.
